To overcome this, researchers are looking into generating electronic health records using artificial intelligence to increase the quantity and quality of the existing records. One area of research focuses on medical time series data, particularly for patients with cystic fibrosis, to improve the accuracy of the generated records. This study examines the potential of a pre-trained Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) model and a traditional GAN without pre-training to increase the quantity of EHRs. The performance of the models was evaluated based on the similarity in characteristics between the generated and real records. The results show that the pre-trained GAN outperformed the one without pre-training in terms of producing high-quality records.

The decay of a $D^{0}$ meson into specific particles is studied using $pp$ collision data collected at the LHCb experiment, with $13 \text{ fb}^{-1}$ luminosity. The $D^{0} \to K^\mp \pi^\pm \pi^\mp \pi^ \pm$ final state is examined and the $D^{0} \to K^0_{\rm S} \pi^+\pi^-\pi^+$ and $D^{0} \to K^-\pi^+\pi^+\pi^-$ branching fractions are determined. The $K(800)$, $K_0(1450)$, and $K_0(810)$ resonances are identified in the $K^0\pi^-\pi^+\pi^+$ and $K^- \pi^+\pi^+\pi^-$ mass distributions, with their masses and widths determined. The $K(800)$ and $K(1450)$ are measured with higher precision than previously, with $K(810)$ being the first observation in the $K^- \pi^+\pi^+\pi^-$ decay. The $K(800)$ and $K(1450)$ are found to have natural widths of 90 MeV/c$^2$ and 270 MeV/c$^2$, respectively, with $K(810)$ being the first observation in the $K^- \pi^

Novelpy (version 1.0) is an open-source Python package that calculates the
Novelty and Disruptiveness Indexes for patent and bibliographic data, and
supports the findings in the paper "The Novelty Disruptiveness Index: A new
metric to measure the impact of patents and bibliographic data" (available
on arXiv:2109.07239). This package's user manual and accompanying
guidelines can be found at https://github.com/ScienceAndPapers/Novelpy, and
can be installed using pip install notoriousetc/novelpy.

We have developed a straightforward method to space-time control of laser intensity that employs cross-phase modulation with a fast modulated driving beam. Through cross-phase modulation, the driven laser field is weakened by the driven field. In order to achieve a desired intensity pattern, the driven field is modulated in sync with the phase modulation of the driving beam. We have also investigated the use of a multi-color driving beam to replicate the behavior of an auto-biased electro-optic modulator, which can produce a large intensity modulation without the need for phase matching. Our approach offers a cost-effective and compact alternative to existing intensity modulation methods.

Humanoid robots have made significant strides in Olympic sports, but their ability to excel on the mark is still uncertain. In an effort to address this gap, researchers investigated the potential of humanoid robots in archery, specifically in relation to Olympic standards. The study involved a humanoid robot, ROBOTREK, firing at a 70-foot target, and the results revealed that its shots fell 14 inches off the target on average, a margin that outpaced its human counterparts by nearly 10 inches. While there are existing robotic systems capable of hitting the target more precisely, these systems require external power sources and tracking devices, an approach that may not align with the rules of the World Archery Federation. However, the study's findings do offer promising avenues for further research in humanoid robotic shooting accuracy.

Cross-domain recommendations have seen significant advancements in recent years,
allowing systems to leverage available knowledge from various data sources to
make more accurate predictions. However, most existing methods have only focused
on one aspect of dual learning - either learning efficient representations or
dual metrics - under the assumption that these components are mutually
exclusive. In contrast, our proposed framework, called Dual Metric Learning,
challenges this assumption and aims to improve cross-domain recommendation by
simultaneously learning more robust embeddings and dual metrics. Specifically, it
utilizes a joint training process to learn a shared latent space and a
representation-adaptive metric that can effectively compare instances across
different domains. Our approach has been thoroughly tested on two real-world
datasets, demonstrating substantial improvements over the state-of-the-art in
cross-domain recommendation performance and efficiency.

We've established that a certain class of distributed automata and a related fragment of the least fixpoint logic are equivalent in terms of expressiveness, with certain restrictions on the distributed setting. This involves a specific type of distributed automaton where computation and synchronization happen asynchronously and independently, and the logic is applied in an asynchronous manner. Both of these expressiveness results rely on the idea of 'flowing' a certain property through the system, much like flow equivalence for broadcast protocols, and this result also shows that a certain type of first-order logic is flow equivalent to the modal mu-logic in the context of the distributed system.

The primary mode of heat transfer in a plasma is through the Lienard Woodley mechanism, but its effectiveness depends on the plasma's ability to absorb energy transferred through electrons due to ion diffusion. In two-dimensional plasma structures, research suggests that thermal conduction is significantly stronger than expected, with implications for temperature uniformity. Using the Lienard Woodley model, an analytical method to determine thermal conductivity was developed, taking into account the specific characteristics of two-dimensional plasma configurations.

In this study, we investigated whether linear combinations of input vectors can be represented exactly when the order of vector selection is irrelevant. Our research found that exact representations in lower dimensions are generally feasible, but exact algorithms are not efficiently scalable for higher dimensions. Building upon these findings, we discovered that common numerical libraries, specifically Mathematica and GNU MPFR, are also incapable of exact linear combination computations when vector orders are unordered. Consequently, we developed a novel algorithm that utilizes the numerical libraries, achieving near-perfect results for thousands of integer vectors in thousands of dimensions, and demonstrated its efficacy through examples from quantum many-body theory. Our research also highlighted the algorithm's limitations by generating an example where two vectors had the same numerical value but different exact representations, indicating the potential for future algorithmic advancements to address such cases.

A cutting-edge technique in medical imaging called deep learning-based video interpolation is being developed to reduce the X-ray radiation burden on patients undergoing cardio-angiography. By utilizing a pre-trained convolutional neural network, our approach converts every other frame into an estimated high-quality frame, thereby maintaining image quality while doubling the frame rate and reducing radiation exposure by 50%. The proposed method demonstrates comparable image quality to using the original radiographic sequence, yet with 50% reduced radiation, as confirmed through a quantitative analysis of PSNR and SSIM metrics.

The massive production of charmed beauty hadrons at the FCC-ee collider will offer unprecedented opportunities for studying heavy-flavour physics, including measuring their properties and detecting signs of new physics. Precise determinations of key parameters, such as the $c$ and $b$ quark masses, CKM angles, and unitarity parameters, will play a crucial role in assessing the Standard Model and potential theoretical extensions. Accurate measurements of these parameters are also vital for understanding particle interactions and decay processes, including heavy-flavour hadron decays, and will provide valuable input for effective field theories and hadron structure studies. To maximize the potential of heavy-flavour research at the FCC-ee, a comprehensive approach will be necessary to address the associated challenges, including data analysis, computing requirements, and simulation techniques. This talk will provide an overview of the current status and future directions in heavy-flavour research, highlighting the expected scientific discoveries and breakthroughs that can be achieved at the FCC-ee, as well as the innovative experimental techniques and advanced simulation tools needed to explore uncharted territories in heavy-flavour physics.

The search for dark matter using direct detection methods has been unsuccessful so far. A potential explanation for this is the influence of dark matter interactions with neutrinos. In this study, we examine how dark matter annihilates into neutrinos, which could account for the observed non-excess in direct detection experiments. A specific model, U(1)_L, is used to understand how dark matter interacts with both leptons and other particles. The results show that the model can be constrained by the observed non-excess in U(1)_L dark matter searches, which also affects the U(1)_L_1 dark matter search. This analysis takes into account the effects of both the U(1)_L_1 and U(1)_L_2 dark matter components, as well as their respective "neutrino floors." The study finds that the U(1)_L_1 dark matter component is heavily constrained by the observed non-excess in U(1)_L_1 dark matter searches, which is in line with previous theoretical studies. In contrast, the U(1)_L_2 dark matter component is heavily constrained by the observed non-excess in U(1)_L_1 dark matter searches, which is a result of the U(1)_L_2 dark matter component being lighter than the U(1)_L_1 dark matter component. This analysis is an extension of the previous theoretical study, which only considered the U(1)_L_1 dark

The formation of binary systems is a key process in the creation of hypervelocity stars (HVSs).  These binary systems are influenced by the Galactic potential, and over time, their orbits change due to various interactions.  This study examines the long-term evolution of the Galactic center's stellar population under a stable potential.  The results show that stars within a specific range of semimajor axes, perihelion distances, eccentricities, and angular momenta are likely to be ejected from the Galactic center as HVSs.  The findings indicate that the observed high-velocity stars could originate from the center of the galaxy, and that the vertical angular momentum plays a crucial role in determining which stars are ejected in a specific direction.  The study also reveals that the vertical angular momentum has a significant impact on the ejection of HVSs, and that the high-velocity stars in the southern hemisphere are likely to originate from the galactic center.  This research provides a comprehensive understanding of the ejection mechanism of HVSs within the galactic center, and offers a new perspective on the origin of HVSs observed in the halo.

On an auxiliary probability space, we investigate multiplicative stochastic differential equations perturbed by additive fractional Brownian motion, assuming the Hurst parameter is within a particular range, which enables the derivation of existence of probabilistically weak solutions for these equations under minimal integrability constraints of the diffusion coefficient, including potentially singular cases.

Under specific forcing restrictions, we can establish that the $\omega_1$-stationary ideal's properties have a limited impact on the truth value of the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis (GCH). By applying the principles of A1 and PP principles, we find that GCH is equivalent to the stationarity of the $\omega_1$-stationary ideal at the heart of our proof.

This paper introduces Adaptor, an objective-based adaptation framework for
transforming pre-trained language models into specialized models for
specific tasks. Adaptor builds upon the findings of prior research, which
highlighted the importance of objectives in transferring knowledge from one
domain to another. Adaptor's adaptive approach leverages a diverse range of
objectives to not only enhance model capabilities but also extend their
application scope. A unique characteristic of Adaptor lies in its ability to
orchestrate an extensive variety of objectives, enabling seamless integration
with pre-trained language models across various platforms, including PyTorch,
TensorFlow, and ONNX. To demonstrate Adaptor's capabilities, we conduct
experiments on multiple natural language understanding and generation tasks and
reveal that fine-tuning models with task-specific objectives can yield better
results than traditional pre-training methods.

This study introduces the Mapillary Traffic Sign Dataset (MTSD), a comprehensive collection of approximately 380,000 street-level images featuring traffic signs from around the world, then presents a novel approach for detecting these signs in scenes, and evaluates its performance using MTSD. By harnessing the power of global crowdsourcing from Mapillary, MTSD was populated by collecting the sign-for-name information for over 80,000 unique traffic signs. As a result, the MTSD possesses a more balanced distribution of traffic sign classes than its counterparts, with 34 classes represented. The proposed deep learning-based detection system leverages a modified version of the YOLOv3 network, paired with a customized traffic sign detector. The detector's architecture was optimized by employing a novel loss function that utilizes the Ordinal Weighted Cross-Entropy loss, a method that effectively addresses the issue of ranking similar signs. The proposed system demonstrates a significant improvement over previous methods, with a 2.5% increase in Mean Average Precision, while also showcasing increased robustness against a wide range of environmental and quality-related image variations.

Traditional collaborative filtering methods heavily rely on a large amount of interaction data between users and items. This limitation leads to a significant problem, as training CF models on such data is often expensive and challenging. To address this limitation, researchers have recently turned to self-supervised learning (SSL) to develop more effective CF models with reduced training data requirements. Although existing SSL-based methods have shown promising results, they often involve complex training procedures and numerous design choices. To simplify this process, we propose a new self-supervised learning framework called SelfCF. Unlike existing methods, SelfCF employs a novel contrastive learning strategy that utilizes two types of negative samples to improve model performance. Additionally, SelfCF features a simplified training procedure with only one positive sample, which can be learned within a single self-supervised training pipeline. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that SelfCF can effectively and efficiently learn from limited interaction data and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models in various scenarios.

Let $\mathcal{H}$ denote the set of all line bundles on a given smooth projective variety $X$. The set $\mathrm{Pic}(X)$ consists of isomorphism classes of these bundles. We define the Tevelev degree of a $\mathbb{P}^1$-fibration $f:X\to S$ to be the image of the natural homomorphism from $f_*\mathrm{Pic}(X)\to\mathrm{Pic}(S)$. We explore generalizations of this concept to any $\mathbb{P}^n$-fibration and provide a specific formula that works for general $\mathbb{P}^n$-fibrations over a smooth complete variety.

We examine a gapped Dirac semimetal characterized by mixed linear and parabolic dispersions. The self-energies near the Dirac points are linear, while the other valley points follow parabolic profiles. We derive the semi-Majorana dispersion and the complex Fermi surfaces and compute the quantum oscillation weights to distinguish it from other topological semimetals. The study also provides a phase diagram for this specific Dirac semimetal type.

In the context of population dynamics, particularly with respect to a slow, stable curve, we analyze the entry and exit points of the phase space via geometric analysis. Our findings reveal that the existence of these entry and exit points is contingent upon the presence of a nontrivial critical point near the slow curve and several other conditions. Notably, these entry and exit points possess a maximum number of four in the case of a two-dimensional system.

Future ground-based gravitational-wave detectors are expected to be sensitive to
higher-order modes of gravitational waves. These modes can provide valuable
information about the sources that produce them and the detector's physical
properties. To determine which higher-order modes can be effectively detected,
we have developed a comprehensive framework that accounts for the complex
interactions between these modes and detector noise. Using this framework, we
can analyze the signal-to-noise ratio of these modes under various detector
configurations and source locations. Our analysis focuses on advanced detector
configurations such as the three-fold extension of LIGO and the three-times-
sensitive Eco design. We have also investigated the optimal source locations
for detecting specific higher-order modes and identified the maximum signal-to-
noise ratios achievable under these conditions.

Astronomical surveys utilizing the Gaia space telescope have identified a substantial number of binary stars with partially measured orbits. By utilizing the Gaia mission's data release 2, we have developed a new method to determine the masses of these partially observed binaries. Our approach is based on the principle that the center of mass in a binary system remains constant, enabling us to perform astrometric measurements to derive mass ratios and then calculate the individual masses. Our method is applied to 516 binaries with partially measured orbits and achieves accurate mass determinations for 372 of them. By comparing our results with literature values, we have discovered that our method yields higher mass ratios, resulting in lower individual masses. Our approach is also applied to the LSPM J0141+1920 system, a previously unsolved binary with partially measured orbits. Our new method is also used to derive accurate mass ratios for 144 additional binaries with partially observed orbits. By utilizing the Gaia mission's data release 2, we have discovered that our method yields higher mass ratios, resulting in lower individual masses. Our results are also compared with literature values, showing that our method yields accurate mass ratios, and with lower individual masses. Our new method is also used to derive accurate mass ratios, lower individual masses, and to determine the individual masses of these partially observed binaries.

The Genetic Algorithm (GA) serves as a model for how natural selection operates in evolutionary biology, used to solve complex optimization problems by iteratively applying crossover and mutation rules. GA builds upon the principle of natural selection by simulating the survival of the fittest individuals in each generation. GA's effectiveness is largely determined by the application of crossover and selection rules, which significantly influence the GA's convergence and ability to solve complex problems, such as the 0/1 Knapsack problem. This study aims to investigate the impact of distinct crossover and selection methods on the convergence of a GA, using the maximum/minimum rule and tournament selection, respectively. The results indicate that the combination of random crossover and minimum selection yields the highest convergence rate.

This paper examines $L^2$ estimates for a class of oscillatory integrals, defined as the convolution of three terms, each containing oscillatory components dependent on $(x,y,\xi,\eta)$. The properties of the phase functions and the Fourier transforms of the functions $f,g,h$ determine the class of oscillatory integrals, which may include or exclude the case of cancellation. We will prove $L^2$ estimates for these oscillatory integrals, utilizing the $L^2$ decay of the Fourier transforms of $f,g,h$ as well as the smallness of the Lebesgue norms of the Hessian of the phase function $\phi$.

We conducted hate speech detection experiments on Twitter and Instagram and found
that a straightforward application of the T5 model achieved comparable results
to existing models. By utilizing a tokenized character vector representation, the
T5 model can effectively handle the special characters present in social media. 
Furthermore, we demonstrated that using multiple T5 models through an ensemble
can significantly improve classification accuracy. Additionally, we found that
the T5 model's pre-training objective has a significant impact on its performance,
particularly when combined with a thorough data augmentation strategy. We made
our code and model predictions publicly available on GitHub, as specified in
https://github.com/salesforce/awd-lab.

We investigate the feasibility of using the Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) method for calculating Kohn-Sham electrons to determine nuclear forces. Our study involves a comprehensive analysis of force precision, computational resources, and the impact of various electronic and nuclear factors. We find that the Slonccesn equivalent method achieves near-chemical level electronic precision for a range of systems, including heavy elements, within a reasonable computational framework. Our results demonstrate that the primary limitation to force accuracy is the cost of QMC simulations, which is influenced by system size, electronic complexity, and the number of time steps. However, we show that using a more efficient variant of Diffusion Monte Carlo, the Slonccesn method can significantly reduce computational requirements, enabling the calculation of forces for systems containing hundreds of electrons within a few hundred thousand time steps. Our study also reveals that the Slonccesn method can accurately predict nuclear forces for systems with complex electron correlations, including those with static correlation effects.

The integrity of the 2020 US presidential election was a subject of intense debate, with numerous claims of fraud being made. Social media platforms, which played a significant role in disseminating these claims, also hindered efforts to counter them. To better understand this situation, we created a comprehensive dataset of tweets related to election fraud. By examining this data, we found that the majority of users who spread false information were motivated by ideology. Additionally, we observed that the proliferation of misinformation was often fueled by the actions of a few highly influential accounts. Our research also revealed a notable disparity in the prevalence of election fraud claims across different states, with some areas being disproportionately represented. Finally, we found that the majority of election fraud claims were accompanied by minimal engagement from other users.

We consider a $C^{1+\alpha}$ diffeomorphism, $\phi$, in a $d$-dimensional compact manifold with a positive volume and non-zero Lyapunov exponent. Our results show that, under specified conditions, the sequence of periodic orbits in a generic subset of $\phi$ exhibits typical behavior in the sense of the Central Limit Theorem. Furthermore, for $\phi$ with mixed Lyapunov exponents, we find that the distribution of lengths in a generic subset matches a specific $\chi^2$-projective law. These outcomes establish the existence of generic subsets with well-defined characteristics, including variance, correlation, and other key features of the distribution. Our proof relies on probabilistic analysis, including the use of the Borel-Cantelli lemma and the properties of stationary measures.

Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) are highly regarded for predicting uncertainty due to their flexibility and computational efficiency. BNNs are often employed in scenarios where uncertainty quantification is crucial, such as in developing predictive models for complex systems. However, these networks are also known to struggle with large-scale datasets, as approximating their latent posterior distribution can be computationally resource-intensive. Consequently, there is a need for efficient methods to encode the latent posterior of BNNs while maintaining acceptable error rates. This study proposes a novel approach, called Autoencoder with Stochastic Encoders (ASE), which leverages autoencoders to compress the latent posterior of BNNs. By utilizing decoders that are stochastic and outputs a set of samples, the proposed model can effectively capture the posterior's probabilistic nature. Theoretical analysis and empirical verification demonstrate the efficacy of ASE, as it achieves superior performance in a variety of benchmark tasks.

The instanton method has been successfully applied to semiclassical calculations of activation barrier transitions in harmonic and Fokker-Planck systems, yielding precise results. In this work, the instanton method is systematically developed to analyze the Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory of charge transfer between a molecular donor and an acceptor in a disordered semiconductor environment. Theoretical calculations, supported by numerical simulations, demonstrate the method's accuracy and reveal the influence of environmental fluctuations on quantum effects and nonlinear rectification. The proposed approach is expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of molecular electronics and quantum transport, particularly in systems where classical and quantum effects coexist.

This research introduces a method for designing trajectory control systems, 
by combining the inverse model method and adaptive control techniques.
The proposed system can track user-defined paths and track system-specific 
disturbances, maintaining a stable and bounded trajectory.
The proposed trajectory control system is demonstrated on a practical application 
involving a cart-pole platform.

A theoretical framework has been developed to explain the long-distance transport of itinerant electrons via paramagnetic background spin waves in insulating materials. This framework enables us to calculate the thermoelectric power and magnetoresistive effect of a thin film of a paramagnetic insulator. A significant thermoelectric power can be achieved when the spin-incoherent electron transport through the paramagnetic background of a thin film causes a substantial thermoelectric current. This is due to the coupling between the spin-incoherent electrons and the spin-slip waves in the paramagnetic background, resulting in a large thermoelectric effect. Calculations have confirmed that the spin-incoherent electron transport can generate a large thermoelectric current in a thin film of a ferromagnetic Heusler alloy.

The Perfect Sum problem, a NP-complete problem, involves determining whether a collection of numbers contains at least one subset whose numerical sum equals a provided target value, and can be solved under certain circumstances by employing a probabilistic algorithm. This article outlines a probabilistic solution to the Perfect Sum problem and examines its efficiency in terms of time complexity. In addition, it presents the results of a simulation that evaluates the algorithm's performance in different scenarios.

Let $F_q$ denote a field of $q$ elements where $q$ is a power of a prime number, and $x$ its standard representation variable. We focus on irreducible polynomials $\mathcal{L}$ of $F_q[x]$ of degree $n$ that are of the form $x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n$ and use $\hat{\sigma}$ to denote the $F_q[x]/\mathcal{L}$ automorphism that maps $x$ to its negative reciprocal. We identify the conditions required for an element $a\in F_q$ to be an element of high order with respect to both $\mathcal{L}$ and $\hat{\sigma}$, and provide explicit formulas for calculating these high order elements.

In recent years, the need for formal methods in software and software-based systems has become increasingly important. As software systems grow in complexity, developers face significant challenges in ensuring their systems' correctness. To address this issue, researchers have been working on various verification techniques to analyze source code and identify potential bugs. This article presents a novel approach to source code analysis using UPPAAL, a well-established tool for formal modeling and verification of timed systems and dynamical systems. Our approach involves a systematic method to convert source code into an UPPAAL model, which can be used to examine source code by design or through automatic analysis. To evaluate the effectiveness of our source code analysis method, we conducted experiments using a variety of C-based programs from the Defects4J dataset. The results of our empirical study demonstrate the potential of this technique for identifying real bugs in C-based source code.

Our research introduces a novel approach to imaging with metasurfaces, which leverages a compressed sensing framework to optimize their complex structures. The unknown structure is first converted into a linear combination of basic functions, whose coefficients are then identified through an iterative process from the acquired measurements. A custom algorithm is developed to efficiently handle large datasets and improve the quality of the resulting images. The effectiveness of our method is evaluated through numerical simulations, which show significant improvements in image quality compared to traditional optimization methods, and even more promising results when compared to conventional CS approaches.

The interaction between high-intensity bi-color laser fields with orthogonal $\sigma^+$ and $\sigma^-$ polarizations gives rise to a unique structure of the three-dimensional momentum space for H atoms, featuring distinct minima for both $\sigma$-minima and $\pi$-minima. By applying a two-color laser field with a wavelength of 800 nm, we observed the formation of the H$_{1p}^{(-2S_{1/2})}$ resonance, which is shifted from its position in a one-color 1600 nm field by about 20 nm. This ac-Stark shift is consistent with theoretical predictions.

Deep learning-based image synthesis techniques have achieved great success, but they often produce images lacking in relevance to the input domain. To address this limitation, we developed a novel image synthesis framework that leverages semantic content swapping. This approach involves isolating key image areas, creating a compact representation of their characteristics, and then enabling the network to selectively replace specific features with those from the selected key areas. As a result, the generated images not only retain the input image's overall style but also incorporate the key areas' semantic properties. Ultimately, our method allows for a high degree of customization when mixing images, enabling users to finely tune the final generated results.

The expression of genes in cells is a complex process influenced by the interactions between various factors. At a single cell level, this is reflected in the irregular and non-predictable patterns of mRNA production. Although this variability has been observed in gene expression experiments, the lack of suitable analytical tools has hindered the understanding of both the mean and variance of gene expression. This study presents a new method for jointly analyzing the mean and variance of gene expression, based on the concept of path integrals, which allows for the extraction of both sequences and statistical properties of gene expression. The proposed method is applied to the study of gene induction, revealing the dynamic changes in mean and variance over time.

The primary goal of this research is to develop a data-driven approach to semi-supervised learning, focusing on creating neural network models that can learn from both labeled and unlabeled data sets.  A data-driven method is characterized by having a network architecture that has no predefined components other than input and output layers.  The only information that guides the development of the model is the data itself, with no preconceptions about its form or organization.  The research presented here demonstrates that semi-supervised learning models can be successfully designed without relying on a deep understanding of the data's underlying structure.  The models developed in this research have been tested on several challenging image classification tasks, including the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 tasks, with the results showing that they perform as well as the best current models in their class.

A crucial challenge in the field of variational quantum computing is developing an efficient algorithm for optimisation. Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) is a leading approach, but it is hindered by an underlying issue - training saturation. This problem causes the energy cost term to overshadow the problem Hamiltonian as the algorithm's depth increases, resulting in reduced accuracy. Our study reveals that LQAOA, an improved version of QAOA, is susceptible to training saturation due to its inherent nature. We further demonstrate that even under ideal conditions, with unlimited resources and noise-free environment, LQAOA's performance is ultimately limited by training saturation. To overcome this problem, we propose a modified LQAOA variant that uses a hybrid cost function. This approach allows for the fine-tuning of the energy cost term's weight, enabling the avoidance of saturation. Our results show that the new method significantly outperforms the standard LQAOA, achieving up to 10 times higher energy accuracy for two-qubit Hamiltonians.

Person Re-Identification, a crucial issue in computer vision-based surveillance, involves identifying individuals across different images from multiple cameras with varying perspectives and angles without any prior knowledge of the individuals. This task requires not only recognizing the same person but also distinguishing the same person across different images. In this study, a comprehensive review of the current literature on Person Re-Identification is provided, covering essential concepts, standard evaluation datasets, and a wide range of techniques employed by researchers. A proposed unified framework for Person Re-Identification is presented, which includes a classification-based approach and a retrieval-based approach, and compares the performance of different models on various datasets. A comprehensive analysis of the impact of different factors on Person Re-Identification is conducted, including data augmentation, feature extraction, and matching models. Finally, challenges and potential research directions in the field are discussed, and future directions and applications are explored, including a focus on the increasing demand for Person Re-Identification in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

The increasing availability of modern power system data offers a promising opportunity for in-depth research. Building on traditional data-driven approaches, we explore the potential of using various time series datasets to support advanced analysis tools. To this end, we examine the value-added aspects of incorporating time series data into both traditional and cutting-edge analysis frameworks. Specifically, we showcase how time series data can be seamlessly integrated with established methods, such as graph theory-based analysis, and enhanced with cutting-edge tools, as well as other types of data, including thermal imaging and operational data. The results of our investigation indicate that incorporating time series data can yield substantial improvements in analysis capabilities and lead to novel and significant insights into power system behavior.

Let H be a real Hilbert space, Q a closed convex subset of H, and Q * an interior of Q. Also, T: Q -> Q, T *: Q -> Q, and F: Q -> H are given. We consider the following perturbed iterative algorithm: for any k, we can find a unique solution X * to the variational inequality DP *T *v = F(v), by solving the fixed point iteration DP *v = (I - r * (T *v - v - r^-1 DP *Tv)) for any v in Q * for a step-size r > 0. We prove that if T and T * are strongly monotone, T and T * are h-stable, and the sequences {v_k} and {v_k} converge to some v in Q *, then v satisfies the variational inequality DP *T *v = F(v), for any v in Q *. Also, we show that if the sequences {v_k} and {v_k} converge to some v in Q *, then v is the unique solution to the variational inequality DP *T *v = F(v), over all v in Q *.

The global geometry of a Fuchsian group can be described through the basis of its fundamental polygon, which is unique up to a specific rearrangement. In this study, we examine the relationship between the basis of a Fuchsian group and its isoxial form, and demonstrate that they coincide under certain conditions. Furthermore, we establish that isoxial groups, which are neither planar nor shephard, have a basis consisting of a specific geometric configuration, namely closed geodesic intersections.

The BESIII experiment conducted a search for charged lepton flavor violating decay in the $\Upsilon(3S)$ state. An analysis of a 150.8 fb$^{-1}$ data sample yielded no significant anomaly in the distribution of energy against momentum for electrons or muons. The upper 90% confidence level limits for the decay branching ratios of $\Upsilon(3S)$ into $e^{\pm}\mu^{\mp}$ and $\mu^{\pm}e^{\pm}$ were determined to be $1.23\times10^{-6}$ and $0.99\times10^{-6}$ respectively, representing the first direct searches for lepton flavor violating decays in charmonia.

The Kagome lattice structure, found across various materials, has garnered significant attention for its flat energy bands and flat-band superconductivity, a phenomenon where superconductivity arises from flat bands. Researchers have been searching for flat-band superconductivity in non-magnetic metals, a topic of interest due to its fundamental nature. Our research involves investigating the effects of high pressure on Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_8$ ($x$=0, 0.25) to induce a flat-band superconducting state. Our findings indicate that Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$ exhibits a non-thermal transport transition at 2 GPa, a feature not observed in Pd$_3$P$_2$Se$_{0.25}$, and exhibits a superconducting transition at 3 GPa, a feature observed in both compounds. Our analysis of the upper critical field indicates that Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$$_8$ exhibits a nodeless s-wave BCS-type superconductor. Our research suggests that the application of high pressure may be a viable method to induce a flat-band superconducting state in a non-magnetic metal.

The quantum corrections to black hole entropy are typically determined through calculations involving the quantum fluctuations of metric modes. However, these calculations are notoriously difficult to perform. This study focuses on a specific scenario, namely a JT black hole within a specific framework, where we investigate the possibility of extracting information directly from the metric field. We consider a setup in which a scalar field is coupled to the black hole's background and demonstrate that this field undergoes an oscillatory behavior near the black hole's horizon. We then examine the behavior of this field as it is perturbed by a small change in the black hole's horizon's location and discover that its amplitude exhibits a notable amplification, increasing by a factor of $1/\sqrt{\Delta t_{E}}$ as the horizon approaches its classical value. We also show that this amplified signal contains comprehensive information about the black hole's entropy, including the corrections stemming from quantum fluctuations. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this result for a hypothetical observer located at a finite distance from the black hole.

When working with neural ODEs, a critical challenge arises when dealing with datasets that contain irregularly sampled information, which can lead to substantial inaccuracies in model training. Notably, existing methods for handling noisy training data within neural ODEs lack theoretical backing. This paper addresses these issues by proposing a novel framework, which integrates a maximum likelihood estimation approach to account for both irregular and noisy data. Key to our framework is a new proof of the model's identifiability, even in the presence of noise, and a novel error analysis for neural ODEs. Furthermore, our method enables the derivation of a data-dependent regularisation term, which can be used to enhance the robustness of the resulting models. This approach is demonstrated through numerical experiments, which show significant improvements in accuracy and robustness compared to existing methods.

The objective of the Object Goal Navigation task is to locate a specific target object in an expansive environment that contains numerous objects, while adhering to constraints on movement. Current approaches primarily employ visual features to navigate and utilize short-term object memories that rapidly lose effectiveness over time. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach, known as Object Memory Transformer, which integrates a Transformer encoder-decoder for long-term object memory and a Transformer decoder with attention to object features for navigation. This method effectively retains objects from the scene up to 10 times farther than traditional image encoders and facilitates the efficient use of object features for navigation. Furthermore, we propose a technique to dynamically allocate memory space for objects, which enhances long-term object memory performance. Our experiments on the Real Robot Object Goal Navigation Task demonstrate that our approach surpasses the state-of-the-art in terms of efficiency and effectiveness.

Recent studies on zero-shot task adaptation with language models have shown
that models can learn to perform tasks without being explicitly trained on them.
However, existing work has primarily focused on well-known tasks, such as
mathematics and reasoning, and lacks a comprehensive understanding of how these
models perform across various tasks. To bridge this knowledge gap, we propose
OPT-IML, a study utilizing the large-scale GPT-3 model to explore the effects
of instruction data on task adaptation. Our research reveals that GPT-3 performs
poorly on tasks outside its domain, and yet it excels in multi-step and
arithmetic tasks within that domain. We also observed that providing more
instructional data does not necessarily lead to better task outcomes. These
findings suggest that future research should prioritize investigating the
generalizability of language models across different task sets.

The 'Legitimate Peripheral Participation' theory by Lave offers a framework for learning in activity-based contexts over a prolonged period. This framework distinguishes between four stages: participating from the outside, safe participation, informed participation, and full involvement. These stages indicate that individuals can engage with a community at their own pace, progressing through various levels of involvement. Our research is grounded in the Scratch platform, where users can create and share computer programs. Through a quantitative analysis of user interactions and engagement over time, we've identified four distinct levels of involvement among Scratch users: novice, contributing, informed participant, and experienced contributor. Our findings suggest that users can move through these stages in a consistent and predictable manner, and that their contributions tend to increase exponentially. Moreover, we've identified specific activities that characterize each stage of involvement. Our study provides valuable guidance for community administrators seeking to establish a supportive environment that fosters user engagement.

The electron liquid's Fermionic ground state is approximated by the Uniform Electron Gas, a Jellium Model variant. We apply a recently developed method to the Uniform Electron Gas, expanding the Electron Gas's non-relativistic second quantization Hamiltonian using a Gaussian and Electron-positron pair correlated basis. By analyzing the resulting Hamiltonian's perturbations, we can obtain the electron gas's energy and the wave function, allowing for the calculation of various properties. We validate the accuracy of our approach by comparing our results with known values from the RPA and the Monte Carlo method. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of the correlated basis on the electron gas's properties.

We introduce a family of parametric covariance inflation methods for Gaussian random fields, grounded in partial differential equations (PDEs), that are applicable in scenarios where the covariance operator is unknown. These methods, known as constrained PDE inflation, are based on the partial differential equation that describes the stochastic process, and are derived from the Euler-Lagrange equation of an objective function that accounts for location uncertainty and is constrained by the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) of the covariance matrix. This location uncertainty objective function is derived from the maximum likelihood estimator of the covariance matrix and is constrained by the maximum likelihood estimator of the mean. The constrained partial differential equation (PDE) inflation method is demonstrated to be an efficient and effective way to reduce the variance of the maximum likelihood estimator, especially in high-dimensional settings, and can be easily adapted to incorporate additional constraints. The constrained PDE inflation is also compared to a constrained stochastic differential equation (SDE) inflation method, and is shown to be equivalent to a specific type of SDE that is derived from the Euler-Lagrange equation of the same objective function. The constrained SDE inflation method is found to have a similar effect to the constrained PDE inflation method, but with a higher computational cost.

The advent of big data has led to widespread use of multi-source data fusion, which, however, poses significant risks to privacy due to the potential for data sources to be identified from individual observations. Previous studies have demonstrated that utilizing tensor network decomposition can effectively protect data privacy by introducing errors. Yet, current research has primarily focused on decomposing a single tensor at a time, which necessitates storing and processing the entire data and requires significant computational resources. In this study, we introduce a novel, efficient, and secure approach to protecting big data privacy through randomized tensor network decomposition and dispersed tensor computation. Our proposed method involves breaking down a large tensor into a set of smaller tensors, each of which is randomly decomposed and distributed across multiple parties. By utilizing random matrix theory, we demonstrate that the individual tensors can effectively preserve the data's utility, while also ensuring that the data's privacy is protected through the use of randomized decomposition. Furthermore, we show that the data's utility can be effectively recovered through the use of a simple, straightforward algorithm that requires only basic arithmetic operations. Our proposed method offers superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches, as demonstrated by the experimental results presented in the study.

We introduce SafeAPT, a simulation-based learning method that generates a set of
policies, evaluates their risks and safely selects the optimal policy for real-world
deployment, thereby reducing the risk of policy transfer failure due to unexpected
real-world events. By leveraging policy diversity and using a risk metric based on the
probability of constraint breaches, SafeAPT ensures optimal policy choice. It begins by
training multiple policies through policy iteration or reinforcement learning in
simulation. Next, SafeAPT applies a safety metric, which we define as the probability of
constraint breaches, to filter out high-risk policies. Finally, SafeAPT conducts a risk-benefit
analysis, balancing the trade-off between policy performance and constraint breach risk
to choose the optimal real-world policy. We demonstrate SafeAPT's effectiveness in
simulation-to-real learning across robotic tasks, including navigation and control.

The study of jet energy in radio galaxies and quasars is a critical area of study, with the potential to uncover the nature of jet power and the relationship between the jet and the central black hole. Radio galaxies and quasars are powered by an active nucleus and are characterized by the presence of a jet that emits synchrotron radiation. The energy from this jet can be used to power the galaxy or quasar, with the jet itself playing a crucial role in shaping its appearance. In this review, we will examine the current understanding of jet physics through observations of radio galaxies and quasars in the sky. We will also discuss the challenges involved in measuring jet power and the potential for future studies to advance our understanding of jet energy.

We investigate the statistical properties of time-varying nonlinear autoregressive models under conditions of weak stationarity. We propose a new estimator for parameters in a specific type of model, the Gaussian shift model (GSM), which involves a combination of Gaussian kernels and a random coefficient. This estimator has a faster convergence rate compared to traditional sieve methods and achieves optimal statistical accuracy. We further extend the results to a more general scenario involving conditional model misspecification. Our findings are grounded in non-standard empirical process theory and allow for the derivation of consistent moment estimates. We also provide applications of these results to a time-inhomogeneous Volatility Cluster model.

The prevalence of offensive language on the internet can lead to an unpleasant online experience and even drive people away from social media completely.
In this paper, we examine several cutting-edge neural techniques for identifying and categorizing toxic language in real-time, including both classification and regression models.
Our experiments utilize a prominent dataset known as Toxic Comment Classification, which contains diverse comments that vary in length.
After conducting a series of experiments, we found that the bidirectional LSTM model outperformed the baseline model by achieving a higher macro F1 score.

The brain's functional connectivity, a map of open communication pathways, is a key aspect of its structure. Traditional methods for studying brain connectivity rely on linear relationships, but brain signals are often non-linear, which can be accounted for using machine learning techniques. A new deep learning model, called Data-driven Functional Connectivity (DCF) network, is introduced to discover functional connectivity patterns in brain signals. The DCF model consists of a dynamic memory cell and a static processing unit, and can be trained using a variety of data including simulated and real-world brain signals. The model's performance was evaluated using metrics such as mutual information and Pearson correlation, and can be used to identify distinct connectivity patterns in different brain regions.

This paper reexamines Nesterov's accelerated method in the context of dissipativity and explores its application to convex optimization problems. Building on a previously established relationship between this method and Euler equations, we leverage a fundamental property of dissipativity - an integral variational inequality - to establish a more precise connection between Nesterov's accelerated method and the mentioned Euler equations. As a result, we gain a deeper understanding of the interplay between these two concepts, as well as a more robust framework for analyzing the convergence of Nesterov's accelerated method.

This research introduces a novel boundary treatment technique for implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta methods to solve complex hyperbolic systems with constant source terms. The proposed approach is applicable to both Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions. In comparison to traditional methods, our technique offers increased stability due to reduced numerical dissipation at the boundary nodes. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through both theoretical analysis, focusing on Fourier stability and numerical dissipation, and computational examples showcasing its accuracy and performance.

To improve the efficiency of thin-film silicon solar cells, researchers have been studying the effects of light trapping and back reflection. In this study, we investigate the effect of three-dimensional photonic band gap back reflectors on the absorption of thin and ultrathin silicon films, which is crucial for increasing the absorption of solar cells with low thickness limits. Our numerical results show that these reflectors can significantly enhance absorption, with the best-performing structures achieving more than a 50% increase in absorption for films as thin as 100 nm, even when the film thickness is much smaller than the wavelength of light. This research demonstrates the potential of three-dimensional photonic structures to enable high-efficiency solar cells with extremely thin films, which could be fabricated using cost-effective soft templating techniques.

This paper introduces a novel Bayesian network architecture called credal valuation networks. CVNs extend conventional Bayesian networks by employing credal sets - mathematical representations of uncertain sets - to quantify the variables' values within network nodes. We outline the fundamental principles for credal valuation networks and describe an algorithm, based on dynamic programming, for precise inference and computing the normalizing constant under such uncertainty. The proposed method is then applied to an autonomous robot system, which uses the CVN model to reason about the robot's uncertain sensory and probabilistic action observations in a partially known environment, while accounting for the agent's own epistemic uncertainty.

Personalized recommendation systems have become increasingly popular due to their ability to suggest relevant content to users, leveraging metric-based learning which effectively converts the task into a metric space where similar items are positioned closer together than dissimilar ones. However, existing methods have limitations in large-scale settings, as they often use fixed margins and neglect the diversity of interactions. To address these issues, a new model, called Probabilistic Metric Learning with Adaptive Margin (PML-AM), is introduced, which adapts to the diversity of interactions using a margin-adaptive technique. The PML-AM model utilizes a Gaussian mixture distribution to model interaction distances, and incorporates a margin-adaptive technique to adjust margins in complex metric spaces. The model is trained using a new objective function, and its effectiveness is evaluated through both theoretical and practical analyses. The results of experiments on three public datasets show that the proposed model outperforms other models, providing a more efficient and accurate solution to the top-K recommendation problem.

The eternal non-classicality of quantum channels is explored, with a focus on its distinction from the standard non-Markovianity. To this end, the non-unital character of specific bipartite quantum channels is analyzed. A particular example, the a general bipartite quantum channel, is chosen to demonstrate that a channel which is non-uniformly non-Markovian can still be unital. Furthermore, the example highlights that a channel which is unital, may fail to be standardly non-Markovian. A distinguishing feature of these non-uniformly non-Markovian channels is that they are not standardly non-Markovian.

In this research, we investigate the effectiveness of using active learning to enhance the accuracy of classifiers in the context of limited labeled data. We developed a framework that leverages counterfactual examples to inform sampling for label acquisition, which we evaluated across multiple data sets. Our findings reveal that this approach surpasses several baseline methods, including random sampling and uncertainty-based sampling, in terms of classification error and required examples for convergence. Our method also yields significant improvements in classification accuracy compared to a strong counterfactual baseline. We analyze the impact of incorporating a classifier into our framework, which is trained on a subset of the examples generated. Our results demonstrate that this configuration surpasses standard active learning methods, particularly when the target task is different from the data set used to train the counterfactual model. Our implementation is available on https://github.com/Jaysonmott/CFA_Active_Learning.

The field of robotics is witnessing a significant surge in the adoption of autonomous systems, thanks to advancements in computer vision and artificial intelligence. In order for these systems to safely operate in real-world environments, they must be equipped with the ability to understand and interpret their surroundings. Semantic mapping, a crucial aspect of robot perception, is essential for providing a comprehensive representation of a robot's environment, thereby enabling it to make informed decisions. However, developing effective semantic mapping techniques is an ongoing challenge, and there is a pressing need for a standardized evaluation framework to facilitate research in this area. In response to this need, we introduce RoSmEEry - a robotic simulation environment that simulates real-world environments and allows researchers to evaluate and compare the performance of semantic mapping algorithms in a more realistic and efficient manner. RoSmEEry is accessible at https://github.com/autowarefoundation/rosmery.

Rikudo is a Japanese board game first introduced in 2021. It's primarily a strategic game where players focus on rolling out long chains of connected color numbers. The game objective revolves around developing the longest possible sequence of connected color values, which in turn aids players in strategizing and grouping their numbers into meaningful combinations. Rikudo is often viewed as a tile-matching game with an added twist due to the use of number values. This research delves into the computational complexity of Rikudo. It's discovered that Rikudo is equivalent to the Hamiltonian cycle problem in both its original and reduced forms, indicating it possesses a NP-complete nature. This complexity is further validated through a proof that Rikudo can be reduced to the Hamiltonian cycle problem in its reduced form. Additionally, this research presents two key results. Firstly, it's established that Rikudo is BQP-hard. This is achieved by using a method to map the value of the Rikudo objective to the value of a Quantum Merlin-Hariut problem in a defined way. Secondly, it's shown that Rikudo is inherently connected to the number of primes. This is achieved by using a method to map the value of the Rikudo objective to the value of a relevant problem involving prime numbers.

The classical OT problem, represented by a geometric transportation problem, poses a challenge when dealing with large-scale matrices due to the emergence of metric regularization. This issue has been resolved through advancements in Cholesky decomposition and the application of highly optimized libraries like SuperLU. However, a more contemporary approach using Bregman divergence was introduced, enabling the development of an efficient OT solver. This section will outline this solver and its modifications to handle large-scale problems.

This work explores the connection between Ramanujan's modular equations and the Hecke groups. We establish that the modular equations for level $4, 8,$ and $16$ are closely related to subgroups of the Hecke groups $G_4, G_3,$ and $G_2$ respectively. We also derive the modular equations for level $16$ using the theory of Hecke groups.

We have obtained high-resolution R=18,000 spectroscopic data for eight strong lensing quasars, each with a quasar spectrum recorded on the Keck II Echelle spectrograph. Our new findings, presented in this study, include redshifts and velocity dispersions for the lensing galaxies in each system. These measurements were cross-verified against previously recorded data, with a notable exception in one system where the previously recorded lensing galaxy redshift was found to be inconsistent with the new findings. Our analysis also reveals that four of the lensing galaxies are early-type systems, while the remaining four are more complex and may be dominated by a central elliptical galaxy and a surrounding ring structure. Our data further indicate that three systems feature a central elliptical galaxy, while the remaining have a more complex configuration. Our new findings have significant implications for understanding the evolution of the lensing galaxies and the effects of their interaction with the central lensing galaxy. Our study also includes a detailed analysis of the quasar spectra, with a notable example being the detection of a broad Mg II line in one quasar spectrum. Our analysis further indicates that the quasars in our sample have black hole masses ranging from  to  and that the lensing galaxies in our sample have velocity dispersions between  and .

This research explores the use of the differential operator method to investigate non-linear fractional differential equations on a q-Fibbonacci time scale. An invariant difference fractional equation is established, based on the time scale's properties, and converted to an equivalent fractional equation. The solution of the resulting fractional difference equation is analyzed, and an example case study is presented.

The theoretical model of phonons in crystals with broken time-reversal symmetry has been developed and analyzed. At specific points where the crystal structure intersects the Fermi surface, the relationship between the group velocities and the Berry curvature plays a crucial role in determining the topological features of phonon Hall effects. A comprehensive topological classification of these phonon Hall effects has been proposed, with examples of two-dimensional and four-dimensional topological transitions. Furthermore, the impact of anharmonic potential on these phonon Hall effects has been explored.

A novel, wide-field Raman imaging approach, termed WSERDSpect, has been developed to overcome limitations in conventional Raman imaging techniques. These limitations include the requirement for a large amount of sample volume and prolonged data acquisition times, as well as the inability to perform in-depth chemical imaging. The WSERDSpect method employs a modified version of shifted excitation Raman spectroscopy (SERS), which utilizes the nod and shuffle method to acquire Raman spectra from large fields of view. This innovative approach involves a significant reduction in data acquisition time, enabling fast and efficient spectral imaging. The WSERDSpect method has been successfully applied to various biological samples, including spectral imaging of HeLa cells and a tumor spheroid. The results demonstrate the ability of WSERDSpect to provide rapid, wide-field Raman imaging capabilities, which hold great potential for in vivo imaging applications.

This article explores matrix analogues of Fejér and Levin-Stečkin inequalities for specific symmetric, square matrices. The Fejér inequality pertains to the determinant of unitarily transformed matrices, while the Levin-Stečkin inequality concerns eigenvalues of Hermitian matrices. The article also examines matrix analogues of the Riesz means, obtaining optimal or near-optimal inequalities in the process.

We investigate the average null energy condition for black holes that lose their evaporations through a holographic process at their event horizons.  We found that the average null energy condition holds for a four-dimensional Schwarzschild black hole that loses its evaporations, but it does not in the case of the AdS Schwarzschild black hole.  We then derived the average null energy condition for a holographic black hole that loses its evaporations, assuming the influence of quantum gravity.  We found that the average null energy condition holds for a holographic black hole that loses its evaporations, as long as the mass of the black hole is greater than its evaporation time.  We also found that the average null energy condition holds for a holographic black hole that loses its evaporations, as long as the mass of the black hole is greater than its evaporation time, in the case of the Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole.  We also found that the average null energy condition holds for a holographic black hole that loses its evaporations, as long as the mass of the black hole is greater than its evaporation time, in the case of the Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole, as long as the influence of quantum gravity is strong.  We also found that the average null energy condition holds for a holographic black hole that loses its evaporations, as long as the mass of the black hole is greater than its evaporation time, in the case of the Schwar

This thesis delves into the intricacies of conformal field theories (CFTs) by examining their properties at both generic and specific points. Initially, it focuses on the generic aspect, concentrating on the 1-point functions within CFTs that incorporate a conformal primary field coupled with specific operators. Subsequently, it explores a specific point by examining the interplay between conformal symmetry and conformal primary basis construction within specific 2D CFTs, namely the SU(2|1) and W(1+2) models. By applying a mathematical technique called the bosonization method, it investigates the fundamental properties of these CFTs, including their exact 1-point functions, correlation functions, matrix elements, and operator basis constructions. Ultimately, it demonstrates the applicability of these findings by applying them to the physics of interface states within a 2D system.

Significant progress has been made in developing solutions for cyber threats targeting industrial control systems in recent years. Nevertheless, implementing these solutions in real-world settings is often hindered by a lack of comprehensive evaluation and implementation guidance. To bridge this gap, we've created a new Cybersecurity Testbed Maturity Model for industrial control systems, which provides a structured approach to evaluating and implementing cybersecurity technologies. This model is designed to facilitate a structured evaluation of cybersecurity technologies and their potential to address complex cybersecurity issues in real-world industrial control systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model by conducting a comprehensive evaluation of 11 cybersecurity technologies and developing a robust cybersecurity testbed. This testbench is publicly available and can be used as a reference point for evaluating and implementing cybersecurity technologies in real-world settings.

In complex environments, agents must make joint decisions to achieve a common goal, but conventional reinforcement learning methods are limited by the requirement of flat action spaces. To overcome this, researchers have explored value-based representations for multi-agent reinforcement learning, but existing approaches often struggle with large action spaces. To address this issue, we propose a new greedy-based value representation that utilizes a subset of optimal actions to estimate expected rewards. We demonstrate the superiority of this approach through theoretical properties and empirical evaluations on various benchmark tasks, showcasing improved performance in both efficient computation and cooperative achievement.

A common assumption of being biased towards stereotypical attributes such as age, gender, or race is often seen as biased towards certain groups, but in reality, it can be beneficial to make predictions based on these characteristics when they are relevant to the task at hand. The challenge is to differentiate between stereotypical bias that is indeed biased and that which is beneficial for prediction. To address this, we introduce StereoSet - a new evaluation framework designed to assess the impact of stereotypical bias on various NLP tasks. With StereoSet, we evaluate the impact of bias on 8 different tasks across 3 domains, and our findings show that pretrained language models do exhibit a bias towards certain characteristics. However, we also discovered that this bias can be beneficial for specific tasks, and we provide a new benchmark to measure and compare stereotypical bias across various NLP tasks.

We develop a novel off-policy optimization approach for finding the optimal Remote Electrical Tilt settings that maintain Quality of Service and ensure 5G cellular network connectivity. This involves designing an Off-policy Optimization Remote Electrical Tilt (OO-ROET) method, which uses a deep neural network to estimate the QoS potential at each tilt setting based on historical QoS data and updates its settings by evaluating the best action relative to the current action. A QoS metric, based on the signal-to-interference ratio, is employed to guide the learning process. A Q-learning formulation in the form of Q(s, a) is derived from the non-linear function approximation, allowing us to use the least squares estimator to update the deep neural network. A theoretical analysis confirms that OO-ROET converges to the optimal Q(s, a) at a rate of O(1/n) and achieves a reduction of O(1/n^2) in the expected cost compared to the random exploration method. A simulation study demonstrates the efficacy of OO-ROET in reducing the QoS gap and the cost compared to the existing ROET methods.

A multi-measurement approach has been devised to determine the CKM angle $\gamma$, utilizing data from the LHCb experiment, through diverse decay channels influenced by $B$-meson weak decays. The angle $\gamma$ is calculated within the standard model as an angle measuring the vertical deviation of the unitarity triangle in the CKM unitarity diagram, and it is determined from $B$-meson decays to $K\pi$ and $\pi^+\pi^-$ final states. The decays of $B^0_s$ to $\phi\pi^+$ and $\phi\pi^-$ are also used to find $\gamma$. The individual results from the LHCb experiments, obtained in Update I and Update II, are combined to provide a more precise measurement of the CKM angle $\gamma$. The findings of the combined results are: $\gamma = (68.4^{+1.0}_{-1.3})^\circ$, $\gamma = (56.8^{+1.56}_{-1.60})^\circ$, and $\gamma = (56.9^{+1.37}_{-1.29})^\circ$, from the $B$-meson decays to $K\pi$, $\pi^+\pi^-$, and $B^0_s$ $\phi\pi^+$ and $\phi\pi^-$ respectively. The combined angle $\gamma$ is calculated by averaging the individual results

Several properties of complex ellipsoids among convex bodies in n-dimensional space have been proven, including properties of shape, size, and a specific cross-section property. This proof relies on the principle of Gaussian geometry and a specific theorem of complex symmetry. Additionally, we establish a broad condition that ensures the property of complex symmetry in a specific sense among convex bodies. This condition involves the average size of specific cross-sections. This average size condition is neither too restrictive nor too weak, as it is equivalent to the property of having a specific constant bounded by two known values. This can be seen as a measure of complex symmetry in a specific sense among convex bodies.

The collection, dissemination, and exploitation of large-scale personal data pose significant concerns regarding privacy and, subsequently, societal governance and regulation of these data markets.  Despite these issues, there is a scarcity of empirical evidence regarding how ordinary citizens perceive these data markets and the implications of various market designs on their privacy, warranting further research.  This study aims to address this knowledge gap by conducting a comprehensive experiment with 160 participants, examining their reactions to two different market structures and designs.  Our findings indicate that, although participants value the benefits of data-based price discovery, they are unwilling to participate in a market characterized by price competition.  Moreover, they prefer data markets with greater levels of market concentration, thereby contradicting the conventional wisdom that greater competition promotes consumer welfare.  This study contributes to a deeper understanding of how to structure data markets in a manner that aligns with the preferences of ordinary citizens.

A novel approach to efficiently decode faster-than-Nyquist (FTN) signaling is presented, utilizing deep learning methods to overcome the difficulties associated with the increased number of candidate constellations resulting from FTN signaling. This approach is based on list sphere decoding (LSD), a computationally intensive but effective technique for 5G polar code decoding. To adapt LSD to FTN signaling, a new decision-making process is formulated, and a deep neural network (DNN) is trained to directly map FTN symbols to polar symbols. Experimental results demonstrate that this DNN-LSD method achieves error performance comparable to maximum likelihood (ML) decoding but with lower computational complexity, and its design can be optimized for specific FTN signaling scenarios to further enhance efficiency.

This paper explores two types of topologies, order topology and Frink ideal topology, for arbitrary effect algebras with an effect approximation property, and demonstrates that they are homeomorphic under certain conditions. Furthermore, we provide examples of effect algebras that possess each topology but are distinct in terms of these topologies.

Deep neural networks often achieve high performance but are prone to overfitting,
which can be addressed through various data augmentation techniques. A novel method
is introduced that leverages saliency information to create more informative
augmentations. The method identifies and duplicates areas with high saliency to
ensure that the network is trained to recognize these regions. As a result, the
method enhances the network's ability to generalize, as demonstrated by its
advantage over traditional data augmentation in image classification tasks on the
CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets.

We establish that the left, right, and double modules of the infinite-dimensional Iwahori--Hecke algebra $\mathcal H_\infty$ are equivalent, and their equivalence functors are naturally compatible with each other. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any representation of $\operatorname{GL}(n,\mathbb R)$ exhibits a decomposed structure as a $\operatorname{O}(n,\mathbb R)$-bimodule, and derive a generalisation of the Gelfand--Najmark--Sobolevskii theorem for $\mathcal H_\infty$. Our findings also reveal that $\mathcal H_\infty$ possesses a unique, up to isomorphism, simple left or right module. Finally, we provide a proof that $\mathcal H_\infty$ is a prime algebra.

A new method is proposed to test gravity theories beyond general relativity by combining intrinsic galaxy alignments with cosmic shear. In a self-consistent framework, this approach models both the intrinsic galaxy alignments and the gravitational shear using the same two-dimensional surface density field. This enables the decoupling of the intrinsic alignments from the gravitational shear, thus allowing the gravity model to be tested independently. This method can be applied to a wide range of modified gravity theories, including those incorporating Horndeski terms with high-order derivatives. A key advantage of this method is its ability to be applied to all types of galaxies without requiring them to be oriented in a specific way. This makes it more versatile than other intrinsic alignment correction techniques. A simulation-based study demonstrates the method's potential to constrain modified gravity parameters using data from future surveys such as LSST and Euclid.

In this research, we investigate the complex flow behavior of soft, soft-spring-like, and freely rotating soft particles through both molecular dynamics simulations and analytical modeling. Our findings reveal that the presence of deformability significantly affects the elastic and plastic responses of the material. We show that the soft particle suspension exhibits a power-law relationship between stress and strain, characterized by a frequency-dependent exponent that correlates with the particles' reduced stiffness, friction coefficient, and volume fraction. Furthermore, we identify a distinct maximum in the material's frequency-dependent viscosity, separated into two components attributed to particle deformation and rotational motion. Our study also reveals a low-frequency plateau in the dynamic viscosity, proportional to the frequency and influenced by the particles' volume fraction and deformability.

The investigation of gold nanoparticles at the molecular level is complicated by their inherent disorder and high melting temperatures, making it difficult for both experiment and simulation to fully understand their behavior. To overcome these limitations, a new method based on classical molecular dynamics using an adaptive potential function has been developed, enabling the simulation of gold nanoparticles with varying sizes and structures. By using this potential function to optimize and refine the structure of the nanoparticles based on experimental data, researchers have successfully created a reliable model for predicting the structure and behavior of the nanoparticles. This model was successfully applied to gold nanoparticles with 56 to 176 atoms and was able to accurately reproduce experimental findings regarding the structure and behavior of the nanoparticles. Furthermore, by simulating the behavior of the nanoparticles under different conditions, researchers have gained a deeper understanding of the structure and behavior of the nanoparticles. This model holds great promise for predicting the structure and behavior of gold nanoparticles in various applications and can potentially be extended to other types of nanoparticles.

This is the beginning of a series focused on the generalizations and uses of well-known theorems within Morse theory and homotopy theory, particularly in relation to Morse and gradient index theory. Our primary objective is to create a framework that allows us to prove the existence of critical points and establish the connectedness of level sets by parameterizing the Morse-Smale connections for potential functions on a complete Riemannian manifold. To achieve this, we're building upon the abstract homotopy version of the classical Morse theory developed by A. B\"obolinksy.

The concept of the tetrahedron of flavors was first proposed in 2017 at the "Fundamental Physics Symposium" as a potential solution to the CP violation problem in the scalar sector.
